I have told this story a hundred times, so stop me if it gets long. Twenty years ago I decided to walk home from the harbor instead of taking the bus.
You decided to walk. At night?
At night, in November. And I remember thinking it was a terrible idea about four minutes later, when it started raining.
So it was raining and you were alone. Did you keep walking?
I kept walking, and then I stopped to look at a doorway I had passed a thousand times. There was a name carved into the stone.
A name you knew. Out of nowhere.
My grandmother's name. That was the turning point of the whole year, not just the evening. I lingered there for an hour, and I could not stop looking at it.
I stopped to look, and then I could not stop looking.
Looking back, that afternoon was the turning point of the trip.

Every good travel story has the same four moves, and most people only ever do two of them. First you set the scene: where you were, what time of day it was, and one detail that puts the listener beside you. Then you keep the ordinary part short. Nobody remembers the bus. Third, and this is the move people skip, you pause right before the turning point. One second of silence, and everybody leans in. Finally you reveal what changed, and then you stop talking. Do not explain the meaning. Let them find it. A story that explains itself is a story nobody repeats.

It was the last morning, and I had one hour before the airport. I remember standing in the square with a coffee, deciding to do absolutely nothing. Then an old man sat down beside me and started to talk. He did not ask where I was from. He asked whether I had seen the church at the end of the street, the small one, not the famous one. I said no. He kept talking about it for ten minutes: the layers under the floor, the door that came from a ship. Eventually I stood up and ran to see it, and I nearly missed my flight. Twenty years later, that church is the only thing from the whole trip I can still see with my eyes closed.

First she set the scene: the last morning of the trip, one hour before the airport, a coffee in her hand. Then an old man sat down beside her and started to talk about a small church at the end of the street. After a while she noticed that she had stopped listening politely and had started listening properly. At that point she stood up and ran to see the church, and she nearly missed her flight. Looking back, that half hour is the only part of the whole trip she can still see with her eyes closed.
